This is NOT the point of Schrodinger's cat, and it is NOT how it works. I've lost interest at this point, since this faux pas is just too much.

The idea of Schrodinger's cat is that, since it can't be observed, the cat exists is a "superposition" between living and dead UNTIL you observe it. Essentially, the likelihood of it being alive is just as good as if it were dead... and to accommodate both possible outcomes, the cat MUST exist in both until the very moment it is observed. Like a sine wave, where 1 is alive and -1 is dead, the cat can't be one or the other... because that would eliminate the possibility that the opposite outcome can happen...

In other words, if the cat is alive in the box, there's absolutely NO way it can ever be dead... or vice versa. This means that the theoretical box/poison don't work, which isn't the case. So, the cat MUST exist somewhere between life and death... a quantum superposition of being both alive and dead simultaneously... UNTIL you observe it.

Upon observation, the two realities collapse upon each other and you will see that the cat is either alive or dead. There can be NO reality where you observe it as "both dead and alive" at the same time. This is ridiculous and wrong.
Schrödinger's cat was an illustration of the silliness of the Copenhagen interpretation. It was definitely not meant to be taken as a description of reality.

My friends often get frustrated with me when they're trying to argue a position because I constantly play "devil's advocate". And the first time someone pointed it out, I was a little surprised because I hadn't really thought about it before. It got me wondering why I did it. Am I doing it just to be contrary? Do I get some weird enjoyment out of frustrating other people? Do I have some need to be the only one who sounds smart? Do I genuinely think people are wrong most of the time?

The answer is none of those. I challenge people's arguments for much more important reasons: Firstly, it makes them better at debating their positions. I challenge people's arguments more when I agree with them, because I want them to really think about the issue and how best to explain/discuss/argue/educate/debate it to/with other people who maybe don't agree. If I hear anything that's not 100% on message and well-supported, I will mercilessly pick it apart. I will argue semantics. I will make deliberately obtuse analogies to point out why they need to be more specific in their categorization. I don't ever tell someone "No, that's not how that works." Instead, I ask them questions that point out flaws in their logic.

The second reason I challenge arguments is more selfish: I want to figure out exactly what I believe about the subject. If it's something I'm not as familiar with, especially, I'll ask questions designed to give me the most information about the topic and the nuances of use. What kind of connotations are we dealing with? Is there controversy on this subject? If the new information seems to fit my worldview, I try to make sure my assumptions are justified and accurate. If it doesn't seem to fit my worldview, I try to figure out why and either discover that I'd been wrong about something else that colored my reaction, or that there's a flaw in the argument that needs exploring.

So here's an example: I had a friend (let's call her Marissa) who was complaining about how beauty pageants ask women to answer broad questions in a very short amount of time and expect the contestants to be philosophically talented and eloquent enough to give a satisfactory answer. You can't solve world peace or eradicate starvation in 30 seconds. I happen to agree to a certain extent, but then she said "It's so misogynistic that they'd expect that of them!"

And I saw what she was trying to say: pageants are often accused of misogyny and the issue of short but deep answers is a part of that experience. Most people who agree would probably only need to hear this and they'd likely nod right along. That's probably really all she was going for: finding common ground.

But if you just told someone who wasn't already on the same page that a pageant was "misogynistic for making them answer that kind of question" it would probably not set quite right in their minds. What is it about that question in particular that makes it misogynistic all by itself? So I asked her. I could see her stopping and reevaluating the idea, trying to figure out why I didn't just agree with her.

"Isn't it?" she asked, not quite sure where to start. "I dont' know," I said. "I don't think that unreasonable questions are misogynistic by themselves, even if the environment they're presented in is (which we haven't even gotten around to fleshing out yet). Why does it matter that they're women? What if it were a male pageant and they asked the men the same questions with the same time restrictions?"

And I could see that point doing its job. Misogyny, by definition, only applies to how women are treated. So what did she really mean?

"Okay, well sexist, then!" she said initially, but then instantly stopped herself. "Well, I guess it's not even that, since it's the same question in both cases and the answer doesn't have anything to do with their gender."

She paused to try to regain her bearings and figure out the message she was really trying to send. "Okay, so the question itself isn't misogynistic or sexist, it's just a really shitty thing to expect someone to answer."

At which point I said "Okay, I can see good reasons for that argument."

Which still wasn't a statement of agreement, and I could tell she wasn't satisfied. Good! It meant she would continue to refine her argument.

So we debated pageants in general a little, trying to flesh out whether or not they were actually sexist, what the purpose of the pageants was and currently is in society, and how best to formulate a position that covers all of the issues people would likely raise. It took us a fair amount of time.

In the end, we came to an agreement based on a more general position with several caveats and a few distinctions. And that, I think, is one sign of a well-thought-out argument. Things are rarely absolutely black and white. So if your argument is a cut and dry "Drugs are bad, mkay," it's not going to be very accurate, precise, or effective. If instead you were to say "Drug abuse is a problem, but the drugs themselves are just tools, many of which have real benefits in proper doses, including for recreation," then you've made a much more comprehensive and inclusive argument that is much more difficult to shoot down.

So yes, I will continue to play "Devil's advocate" because at the end of the day, it makes us all better at debating things well and getting to the heart of matters more quickly. When you can pinpoint where disagreements stem from, you can address them that much more efficiently.

And nothing harms a cause or message more than a poorly argued position. Even if someone is right, if the reasons they provide for their position are not quite right, or don't actually follow logically, the person they're arguing with isn't going to be convinced, and what's worse is that they might even solidify an incorrect position just because they now associate the correct one with something like ineptitude or bad logic. And it'll just give them more ammunition for their arguments to others, as they then cite the bad arguments as "How people on that side think", even if most of the campaign doesn't actually think that.

Nothing hurts a campaign more than a proponent who argues poorly.

Someone who campaigned for recognizing climate change but whose argument was "Polar bears are cold blooded, which means they cool off the atmosphere, so if we don't stop polluting they'll all die off and the world will get warmer," they'd be laughed at. Someone who was anti-climate-change would have no trouble shooting down that argument, which makes it look like his side wins to anyone who sees/hears that conversation. And he'll probably use that exchange later on as an example of how "out of touch with reality" climate change proponents are. It's not true, of course, and hopefully at some point someone will challenge him to be more accurate, but it can do a lot of damage in the meantime.

And that's a hyperbolic example, of course, just to demonstrate a point. Most of the time the differences in semantics or message are going to be far more subtle, which makes it just that much harder to combat.

Sorry for the wall of text, but I'm trying to take my own advice and be as complete as I can without going way overboard, and I was doing a little self-exploration as well, trying to pin down my own views.

That may actually be useful for them temporarily, so how recent the incident is can make a difference in how best to approach someone.

People will resist ideas contrary to their own mostly if they see it as a confrontation. If they think they're arguing with someone over whether or not they are "right", they'll defend their position as a reaction rather than proactively organizing their stance. So i always try to couch my questions in a way that makes it sound like we're both exploring the issue together, rather than at odds. The best way I've found to do this is to ask them questions as if I want them to explain it to me. If something doesn't sound right or I know it needs attention, I'll pretend it confuses me and ask them to clarify. If they think they're in control of the message, they'll be much more likely to continue the discussion and offer more talking points. And if they refine their argument and get rid of the wrong/confusing/awkward bits along the way, it makes it that much more effective, because now they're convinced they're the ones who have come up with all of this on their own, and they'll defend that so much more strenuously for their familiarity with the subject.
